newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - NYMEX delivery bearish for foreign crude.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NYMEX delivery bearish for foreign crude.

text.p: A large and unusual physical delivery of foreign crude oil against the May NYMEX contract, the first in five years, drives home a long-held market perception that supplies far outpace demand, traders and refiners said on Thursday.
"This just shows how weak the market has gotten," a Gulf Coast trader said.
The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) received a record 6.621 million barrels of total deliveries against the May contract, the highest level since crude futures began trading in New York in 1983.

Of total deliveries, 2.73 million barrels were foreign grades, most of which was Nigerian Bonny Light. The remainder was Brent and Oseberg from the British and Norwegion North Sea sectors, traders said.
Atlantic Richfield co, privately held Swiss trader Vitol and Northridge Energy Marketing Corp, a subsidiary of TransCanada Pipelines Ltd, made the deliveries, traders said.
The last time foreign crude was delivered into the exchange was July 1992, when just 720,000 barrels of a foreign grade were shipped.
Sellers rarely deliver foreign crude into the NYMEX because it is usually uneconomic and is considered the option of last resort.

This month's sizeable foreign delivery reflects the wide transatlantic arbitrage between benchmarks West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent, and the feeble price for 'dated' Brent cargoes, traders said.

The June WTI/Brent spread has been creeping up in recent weeks, reaching $1.55-65 a barrel on Thursday, boosting the incentive to move North Sea and West African barrels to the United States, traders said.

Dated Brent cargoes had been fetching prices at around a $1.00 a barrel discount to International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) futures earlier this month. That price has since recovered to around 35-45 cents discount, mainly because North Sea barrels have been moving into U.S. and Asian markets, traders said.

A longer-term factor behind delivering the foreign barrels on the contract is the improved economics of shipping crude from the Gulf Coast into the hub at Cushing, Oklahoma. It currently costs around 80-85 cents a barrel, down from $1.15-20 a year ago.
This structural change in transport economics suggests that the NYMEX may witness even more foreign deliveries down the road, traders said.
Because the NYMEX did not receive any specific requests for the foreign crudes, the deliveries were allotted in parcels of 80,000 barrels, beginning with the largest 'long' positions.
Though not confirmed by the company, Royal Dutch/Shell received the bulk of the foreign barrels against its large long position, tradres said.

If a company received Bonny Light instead of WTI, it must pay a fixed premium of 60 cents a barrel to account for differing crude qualities. Brent and Oseberg give the company a discount of 30 cents a barrel.

Refiners in or around Cushing, such as Dupont energy unit Conoco and privately held Farmland, were said to be evaluating offers for the foreign barrels, although it was unclear how much their facilities could handle immediately, traders said.
One trader said the alternative NYMEX deliveries highlighted the need for refiners to maintain flexibility in their crude slates.
"This is a very competitive market. You can't afford not be flexible," he said.
